draft.title: Families and slaves in Rome
card: A Roman household was led by the father, called the paterfamilias. He had legal power over his wife, children, slaves and property.
The household included more than parents and children. Slaves who lived and worked there were counted as part of it too.
Slaves did much of Rome's work, such as farming, building, cooking, cleaning and teaching. Many were captured in war, and slaves were owned as property, with few rights.
Some slaves were freed by their owners. A freed slave could become a Roman citizen, though a freed slave could still face limits in public life.
draft.remember: The paterfamilias ruled the household, and slaves did much of the work, though some were freed.

a.q: Who was the paterfamilias in a Roman household?
opts: The father, who held legal power over the household
The eldest son, who managed the family's slaves
The mother, who ran the home and trained the children
The oldest slave, who gave orders to the other slaves
a.why: The paterfamilias was the male head of the household, and the law gave him power over everyone in it. The eldest son is tempting, but a son was still under his father's power.
a.clue: Think about who held legal power over the whole household.

b.q: Lucius owned a farm outside Rome, and slaves worked his fields. One slave, Felix, was freed by Lucius after many years of service. What could Felix become?
opts: A Roman citizen
A paterfamilias of Lucius's house
A consul of Rome
A slave again, by law
b.why: The card says a freed slave could become a Roman citizen. The other options do not fit: Lucius stays head of his own household, and nothing on the card says a freed slave could become a consul.
b.clue: Think about what freedom could give a former slave.

a.best: The father, who held legal power over the household

problems.detail: The card says the paterfamilias had legal power over his wife. By the late Republic most marriages were 'sine manu', so a wife usually stayed under her own father's legal power, not her husband's. The paterfamilias was also the oldest living male, often a grandfather, not simply 'the father'. Better: 'He had legal power over his children, slaves and property, and in some marriages over his wife.'
The clue 'who held legal power over the whole household' repeats the wording of the right option ('held legal power over the household'), so a student can match the words without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The card oversimplifies the paterfamilias: he did not usually hold legal power over his wife in the late Republic, and he was the oldest living male rather than simply 'the father'. Question a's clue repeats the right option's wording and gives the answer away.

proposal.title: Families and slaves in Rome
card: A Roman household was led by its oldest living male, called the paterfamilias. He was often the father, but could be a grandfather.
He had legal power over his children, slaves and property, and in some marriages over his wife. Adult sons usually stayed under his power while he lived.
Slaves were part of the household too. They did much of Rome's work, such as farming, building, cooking and teaching. Many were captured in war and owned as property, with few rights.
Some slaves were freed by their owners. A freed slave could become a Roman citizen, though freed slaves could still face limits in public life.
proposal.remember: The oldest male ruled the household, slaves did much of Rome's work, and some slaves were freed.

a.q: Marcus's father has died. Marcus lives with his wife, his adult son Gaius, Gaius's children and several slaves. Who is the paterfamilias?
opts: Marcus, because he is the oldest living male
Gaius, because he has children of his own
Marcus's wife, because she runs the home
The oldest slave, because he directs the others
a.why: With his father dead, Marcus is the oldest living male, so he is the paterfamilias. Gaius is tempting because he is a father, but adult sons usually stayed under their own father's power while he lived.
a.clue: Gaius has children, but who is still above him?

b.q: Lucius owned a farm outside Rome, and slaves worked his fields. Lucius freed one slave, Felix, after many years of service. What could Felix become?
opts: A Roman citizen
The paterfamilias of Lucius's household
Lucius's property, with few rights
A war captive owned by the state
b.why: A freed slave could become a Roman citizen. Lucius's property is tempting because that is what Felix was before, but once freed he was no longer owned. Lucius stays head of his own household.
b.clue: Think about what freedom could give a former slave.
